metadata.title: China's 2015 Market Crash: A Leverage Feedback Loop

canonical_sources.title: The 2015 Stock Market Crash in China

pedagogy.problem_statement: Why can a price drop turn from ordinary volatility into a self-reinforcing crash?
pedagogy.core_thesis: Margin finance creates a feedback loop: falling prices erode collateral, which forces sales, which further lowers prices in thinner markets.
pedagogy.mental_model: A narrowing funnel: every forced order tries to exit through a smaller pool of buyers.
pedagogy.key_takeaway: Leverage does not cause every decline, but it makes the path down mechanically steeper once collateral thresholds are crossed.
verified_claims: The Shanghai Composite rose by roughly 150 percent from mid-2014 to its June 2015 high.
The Shanghai Composite fell about 32 percent between June 12 and July 8, 2015.
Margin finance exposes investors to forced selling when collateral falls below maintenance requirements.
Chinese authorities deployed a package of interventions in July 2015, including restrictions, liquidity support and state-directed market support.
anti_patterns: Do not attribute the crash to a single cause.
Do not present the simple leverage equation as a claim about every investor's exact leverage.
Do not equate market-capitalisation loss with cash physically disappearing.

equations.spoken_form: drawdown equals the peak price minus the current price, divided by the peak price
equations.context: Describes the size of a decline

equations.spoken_form: equity after a price fall equals starting equity times one minus leverage times the decline
equations.context: Simplified illustration of how leverage magnifies losses

equations.spoken_form: more forced selling lowers the next price, which lowers collateral
